prompt:
A reporting application runs on Amazon EC2 in account A. It must read objects from an Amazon S3 bucket that belongs to account B. The security team does not allow long-term access keys in either account, and the data must not be copied out of account B.

Which solution meets these requirements?

options.text: Create an IAM user in account B with s3:GetObject on the bucket and store its access keys in AWS Secrets Manager in account A
options.explanation: An IAM user's access keys are long-term credentials; keeping them in Secrets Manager hides them but does not remove them.

options.text: Configure S3 Same-Region Replication from the bucket in account B to a new bucket in account A that the application can read
options.explanation: Replication copies every object into account A, which the requirements forbid.

options.text: Create an IAM role in account B that trusts account A and allows s3:GetObject, and have the application assume it through AWS STS
Share the bucket with account A through AWS Resource Access Manager and grant the EC2 instance profile read access to it
options.explanation: AWS RAM does not share S3 general purpose buckets; cross-account bucket access is granted with a bucket policy or a role.

explanation: A role in the bucket's account whose trust policy names account A lets the application call sts:AssumeRole and receive temporary credentials that expire on their own, so no access keys exist anywhere and the objects stay in account B. Access keys in a secret are still long-term credentials, replication copies the data, and RAM is not how S3 buckets are shared. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/id_roles_common-scenarios_aws-accounts.html

prompt:
A company runs 30 AWS accounts in AWS Organizations. The security team must make sure that nobody in any member account, including users with the AdministratorAccess policy, can stop or delete the organization's AWS CloudTrail trails.

Which solution meets this requirement?

options.text: Attach a permissions boundary that denies cloudtrail:StopLogging and cloudtrail:DeleteTrail to every IAM role in the member accounts
options.explanation: Administrators can create new roles without the boundary or remove it, so a boundary on existing roles does not bind them.

options.text: Attach a service control policy to the member accounts' OUs that denies cloudtrail:StopLogging and cloudtrail:DeleteTrail
Deploy the AWS Config managed rule cloudtrail-enabled to every account with an automatic remediation that turns logging back on
options.explanation: AWS Config evaluates after the change happens; logging is off until remediation runs, so it detects and repairs rather than prevents.

options.text: Attach an IAM policy that denies the CloudTrail stop and delete actions to the administrators' IAM group in each member account
options.explanation: Anyone with AdministratorAccess can detach a policy from their own group, so the deny does not hold against them.

explanation: A service control policy sets the maximum permissions for every principal in the accounts it applies to, including administrators and the root user of a member account, and nothing inside the account can override it. A permissions boundary or a group policy can be removed by the very administrators they target, and AWS Config only detects and repairs a trail after it has been stopped. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/organizations/latest/userguide/orgs_manage_policies_scps.html

prompt:
A company has 40 AWS accounts in AWS Organizations and uses a SAML 2.0 identity provider for its workforce. Employees must sign in to the AWS Management Console and CLI of the accounts they work in with their corporate credentials, and the security team wants to define each job function's permissions once and assign them to groups across accounts.

Which solution meets these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

options.text: Create a SAML identity provider and matching IAM roles in each of the 40 accounts, and map the corporate groups to those roles in the IdP
options.explanation: This federates correctly but means building and keeping 40 copies of every role and every mapping in step by hand.

options.text: Create an Amazon Cognito user pool federated with the corporate IdP and an identity pool that issues AWS credentials for each account
options.explanation: Cognito is built for application end users; it does not give a workforce console sign-in across an organization's accounts.

options.text: Create IAM users in a central account with the corporate user names and let them assume roles in each member account
options.explanation: IAM users bring separate passwords instead of corporate credentials, and the cross-account roles still have to be built per account.

options.text: Enable IAM Identity Center with the corporate IdP as its identity source, define permission sets, and assign groups to accounts

explanation: IAM Identity Center connects once to the external SAML IdP, and a permission set is defined once and provisioned as roles into every account a group is assigned to, with a single portal for console and CLI access. A per-account SAML setup works but multiplies the roles and mappings by 40, Cognito targets customer-facing apps, and IAM users do not use corporate credentials. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/singlesignon/latest/userguide/what-is.html

prompt:
A public web application runs behind an Application Load Balancer. Logs show SQL injection attempts in query strings and bursts of thousands of HTTP requests per minute from a handful of IP addresses. The company wants to block both at the edge of the application without changing the application code.

Which solution meets these requirements?

options.text: Associate an AWS WAF web ACL with the load balancer that uses the SQL database managed rule group and a rate-based rule
Subscribe to AWS Shield Advanced and add the load balancer as a protected resource so the AWS response team filters the traffic
options.explanation: Shield Advanced protects against DDoS events; inspecting query strings for SQL injection needs AWS WAF rules.

options.text: Enable Amazon GuardDuty in the account and configure it to block the source IP addresses of malicious requests it finds
options.explanation: GuardDuty produces findings; it does not block requests at the load balancer on its own.

options.text: Tighten the load balancer's security group to allow HTTPS only and add network ACL deny rules for the offending addresses
options.explanation: Security groups and NACLs work on IPs and ports; they cannot see SQL in a query string, and a hand-kept deny list lags new addresses.

explanation: AWS WAF attaches directly to an ALB and inspects each HTTP request: the AWS managed SQL database rule group matches SQL injection patterns, and a rate-based rule blocks any IP that exceeds a request count in the evaluation window. Shield Advanced is DDoS protection that relies on WAF for request inspection, GuardDuty only reports, and security groups and NACLs cannot read request content. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/waf/latest/developerguide/waf-rule-statement-type-rate-based.html

prompt:
Applications in a VPC's private subnets read and write an Amazon S3 bucket through a gateway VPC endpoint. A new security requirement says the bucket must refuse every request that does not arrive through that specific endpoint, including requests from administrators on the internet.

Which change meets this requirement?

options.text: Attach an endpoint policy to the gateway endpoint that allows access only to this bucket and denies every other bucket
options.explanation: An endpoint policy limits what traffic through the endpoint may reach; it does nothing to requests that reach the bucket by another path.

options.text: Add a bucket policy that denies all S3 actions unless the aws:SourceIp condition matches the VPC's private CIDR range
options.explanation: The aws:SourceIp condition cannot be used for requests that reach S3 through a VPC endpoint, so this policy denies the applications too.

options.text: Add a bucket policy that denies all S3 actions unless the aws:SourceVpce condition key equals the gateway endpoint's ID
Enable S3 Block Public Access on the bucket and remove the internet gateway route from the VPC's public subnets
options.explanation: Block Public Access stops public grants, but authenticated IAM principals on the internet can still reach the bucket.

explanation: A bucket policy is evaluated for every request to the bucket, so a Deny with aws:SourceVpce not equal to the endpoint ID rejects anything that did not come through that endpoint, whoever sends it. An endpoint policy controls the VPC side only, aws:SourceIp cannot be used for requests that arrive through a VPC endpoint, and Block Public Access does not stop authenticated callers. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/example-bucket-policies-vpc-endpoint.html

prompt:
A company stores regulated documents in Amazon S3. Auditors require encryption at rest where the company controls who may use the key through its own key policy, can disable the key at any time, and can see every use of the key in AWS CloudTrail. The team does not want to manage key material or encryption code.

Which solution meets these requirements?

options.text: Use server-side encryption with Amazon S3 managed keys (SSE-S3) and a bucket policy that rejects unencrypted uploads
options.explanation: SSE-S3 keys are managed entirely by S3; there is no key policy to edit, no way to disable the key, and no per-use CloudTrail record.

options.text: Use server-side encryption with the AWS managed KMS key aws/s3 and set it as the bucket's default encryption
options.explanation: AWS managed keys log their use, but their key policy cannot be changed and the key cannot be disabled by the customer.

options.text: Use server-side encryption with customer-provided keys (SSE-C) and send the key with each request from the application
options.explanation: With SSE-C the company generates, stores and supplies every key on every request, which is the key management the team wants to avoid.

options.text: Use server-side encryption with a customer managed AWS KMS key (SSE-KMS) and set it as the bucket's default encryption

explanation: A customer managed KMS key has a key policy the company writes, can be disabled or scheduled for deletion, and every encrypt and decrypt call S3 makes with it is logged in CloudTrail, while KMS holds the key material. SSE-S3 offers no key policy, the aws/s3 key's policy is fixed, and SSE-C pushes key handling onto the application. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/UsingKMSEncryption.html

prompt:
An application on Amazon EC2 connects to an Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL database with a user name and password that is currently in a configuration file. A third-party library in the application accepts only a static user name and password. The security team requires the password to be changed automatically every 30 days without a code release.

Which solution meets these requirements?

options.text: Store the credentials in AWS Secrets Manager with rotation every 30 days and have the application read the secret as it connects
Store the password as an AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store SecureString and turn on automatic rotation of its AWS KMS key
options.explanation: Rotating the KMS key changes the key that encrypts the parameter, not the database password stored in it.

options.text: Enable IAM database authentication on the instance and have the application request a new authentication token for each connection
options.explanation: IAM auth replaces the password with a short-lived token the code must generate per connection, which the library cannot do.

options.text: Enable automatic rotation on the KMS key that encrypts the RDS storage and set the rotation period to 30 days
options.explanation: Storage key rotation changes the encryption key for data at rest; the database user's password stays the same.

explanation: Secrets Manager can rotate an RDS secret on a schedule, updating the database password and the secret together, and the application keeps passing a plain user name and password that it fetches from the secret. KMS key rotation changes encryption keys, not database passwords, and IAM database authentication needs code that generates a token for every connection. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/secretsmanager/latest/userguide/rotating-secrets.html

prompt:
A financial services company must keep trade records in Amazon S3 for 7 years in a write-once-read-many (WORM) form. Regulators require that no user, including the account's root user, can overwrite or delete a record before its retention period ends, and that the retention period cannot be shortened.

Which solution meets these requirements?

options.text: Enable S3 Object Lock on the bucket and apply a 7-year default retention period in governance mode
options.explanation: In governance mode a user with s3:BypassGovernanceRetention can delete objects or shorten the retention, so it is not tamper-proof.

options.text: Enable S3 Object Lock on the bucket and apply a 7-year default retention period in compliance mode
Enable S3 Versioning with MFA delete and a lifecycle rule that moves objects to S3 Glacier Deep Archive after 30 days
options.explanation: MFA delete adds a step to permanent deletes but the root user can still delete versions or turn MFA delete off.

options.text: Enable S3 Object Lock and place a legal hold on each object as it is written, removing the hold after 7 years
options.explanation: A legal hold has no retention period and any user with s3:PutObjectLegalHold can remove it early.

explanation: In compliance mode an object version cannot be overwritten or deleted by any user, including the root user, until its retention date, and the retention mode and period cannot be shortened. Governance mode can be bypassed with a special permission, a legal hold can be lifted by anyone allowed to set it, and MFA delete still leaves the root user able to delete. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/object-lock.html

prompt:
A company wants continuous monitoring of its AWS accounts for signs of compromise, such as EC2 instances communicating with known cryptocurrency-mining hosts or API calls from unusual locations, without deploying agents or managing log pipelines.

Which AWS service meets this requirement?

options.text: Amazon Inspector, scanning EC2 instances and container images
options.explanation: Inspector finds software vulnerabilities and network exposure; it does not watch for active malicious behaviour in API and network logs.

options.text: Amazon Macie, analysing the data stored in the account
options.explanation: Macie discovers sensitive data in S3 objects; it does not analyse network traffic or API activity for threats.

options.text: Amazon GuardDuty, analysing the account's logs and activity
AWS Config, evaluating resources against managed rules
options.explanation: AWS Config checks resource configurations against rules; it does not detect compromised instances or suspicious callers.

explanation: GuardDuty is a managed threat detection service that reads CloudTrail events, VPC Flow Logs and DNS logs on its own, with no agents or pipelines, and raises findings such as cryptocurrency-mining traffic or unusual API activity. Inspector looks for vulnerabilities, Macie for sensitive data, and AWS Config for configuration drift. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/guardduty/latest/ug/what-is-guardduty.html

prompt:
A company has hundreds of Amazon S3 buckets created by different teams over several years. The compliance team must find which buckets contain personally identifiable information, such as passport numbers and credit card numbers, and get an ongoing report as new objects arrive.

Which AWS service meets this requirement?

options.text: Amazon Macie with automated sensitive data discovery
Amazon GuardDuty with S3 Protection enabled
options.explanation: S3 Protection watches API calls to buckets for suspicious access; it does not read object contents for personal data.

options.text: Amazon Detective with the S3 data source enabled
options.explanation: Detective helps investigate security findings after the fact; it does not classify what data objects contain.

options.text: AWS Security Hub with the foundational best practices
options.explanation: Security Hub checks bucket settings such as public access and encryption, not the data stored in the objects.

explanation: Macie uses managed data identifiers to find sensitive data such as passport and credit card numbers inside S3 objects, and automated discovery keeps sampling buckets and reporting as data changes. GuardDuty, Detective and Security Hub look at activity, investigations and configuration, not at object contents. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/macie/latest/user/what-is-macie.html

prompt:
A three-tier application has an internet-facing Application Load Balancer in public subnets and application servers on Amazon EC2. The security team requires that the application servers have no network path to or from the internet of their own and accept traffic only from the load balancer.

Which TWO configurations together meet this requirement? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Launch the application servers in private subnets whose route table has no route to an internet gateway
In the application servers' security group, add a deny rule for 0.0.0.0/0 above the rule that allows the application port
options.explanation: Security groups support allow rules only; there is no deny rule to add, and their rules are not ordered.

options.text: In the application servers' security group, allow the application port with the load balancer's security group as the source
In the application servers' security group, allow the application port from the load balancer's Elastic IP addresses
options.explanation: An ALB has no Elastic IPs and its addresses change; it reaches targets from private IPs inside the VPC.

options.text: Add network ACL rules on the application subnets that allow the application port from the load balancer's DNS name
options.explanation: Network ACL rules accept CIDR blocks only, not DNS names, and an ALB's addresses change over time.

explanation: Private subnets with no internet gateway route give the instances no inbound path from the internet, and a security group rule that references the ALB's security group admits traffic only from the load balancer's nodes, whatever their changing IPs. Security groups have no deny rules, ALBs have no Elastic IPs, and network ACLs cannot use DNS names. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/vpc/latest/userguide/security-group-rules.html

prompt:
Developers must be able to create IAM roles for the AWS Lambda functions they deploy. The security team is worried that a developer could create a role with more permissions than the developer has and use it to escalate privileges. Developers must stay self-service.

Which solution meets these requirements?

options.text: Attach a service control policy to the developers' account that denies iam:CreateRole and iam:PutRolePolicy for every principal
options.explanation: This removes the developers' ability to create Lambda roles at all, which breaks the self-service requirement.

options.text: Grant the developers the AWS managed PowerUserAccess policy, which allows all services except IAM user and group management
options.explanation: PowerUserAccess does not let developers create roles, so they could not deploy their functions' roles themselves.

options.text: Allow iam:CreateRole only when the iam:PermissionsBoundary condition names an approved boundary policy, and deny changes to that policy
Run IAM Access Analyzer policy validation on every role developers create and alert the security team about overly broad policies
options.explanation: Policy validation reports problems after the role exists; it does not stop an over-privileged role from being created and used.

explanation: A permissions boundary caps the effective permissions of any role it is attached to. Requiring a specific boundary on iam:CreateRole, and denying edits to or removal of that boundary, lets developers create roles freely while no role can exceed the boundary. An SCP deny or PowerUserAccess takes the ability away entirely, and Access Analyzer validation only reports. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/access_policies_boundaries.html

prompt:
A company serves a static website from an Amazon S3 bucket through an Amazon CloudFront distribution. A security review found that users can also fetch objects straight from the bucket's URL. The company wants the bucket to stay private, with Block Public Access on, and serve objects only through this distribution.

Which TWO actions together meet these requirements? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Create an origin access control (OAC) and attach it to the distribution's S3 bucket origin
Turn on S3 static website hosting and set the bucket's website endpoint as the distribution's custom origin
options.explanation: A website endpoint only serves public objects and does not support origin access control, so the bucket would have to be public.

options.text: Require CloudFront signed URLs on the distribution's default cache behavior for every object
options.explanation: Signed URLs control which viewers may use the distribution; they do nothing to stop direct requests to the bucket.

options.text: Add a bucket policy that allows s3:GetObject to the CloudFront service principal when AWS:SourceArn is the distribution ARN
Add a bucket policy that allows public s3:GetObject only when the Referer header carries a secret value set by CloudFront
options.explanation: This needs Block Public Access off, and anyone who learns the header value can send it straight to the bucket.

explanation: With OAC, CloudFront signs its requests to S3, and a bucket policy that allows the cloudfront.amazonaws.com principal only for this distribution's ARN lets those signed requests in while the bucket stays private behind Block Public Access. Website endpoints need public objects, signed URLs restrict viewers rather than the origin, and a Referer secret requires a public bucket. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonCloudFront/latest/DeveloperGuide/private-content-restricting-access-to-s3.html

prompt:
A company is moving its public web applications behind Application Load Balancers and wants HTTPS everywhere. Certificates last expired unnoticed and caused an outage, so the team wants TLS certificates that renew automatically with no manual steps after setup. The domain's DNS is hosted in Amazon Route 53.

Which solution meets these requirements?

options.text: Buy certificates from a third-party CA each year, import them into AWS Certificate Manager, and attach them to the load balancers
options.explanation: ACM does not renew imported certificates; each one has to be reissued and reimported before it expires.

options.text: Request public certificates in AWS Certificate Manager with DNS validation and attach them to the load balancers' HTTPS listeners
Request public certificates in AWS Certificate Manager with email validation and attach them to the load balancers' HTTPS listeners
options.explanation: Email-validated certificates need a domain owner to act on validation emails, so renewal is not hands-free.

options.text: Upload certificates to the IAM server certificate store and attach them to the load balancers' HTTPS listeners
options.explanation: IAM server certificates are never renewed by AWS; someone has to upload a new certificate before each one expires.

explanation: ACM renews its own public certificates automatically, and with DNS validation the CNAME record left in Route 53 lets ACM prove domain control again at renewal without anyone acting. Imported and IAM-stored certificates are never renewed by AWS, and email validation needs a person to respond. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/acm/latest/userguide/dns-validation.html

prompt:
A team must give a partner's AWS account a copy of an Amazon EBS snapshot. The snapshot is encrypted with the AWS managed key aws/ebs. The data must stay encrypted at every step, and the partner must be able to create volumes from the snapshot in its own account.

Which solution meets these requirements?

options.text: Modify the snapshot's permissions to add the partner's account ID, and have the partner create volumes with its own aws/ebs key
options.explanation: Snapshots encrypted with an AWS managed key cannot be shared with another account at all.

options.text: Edit the key policy of the aws/ebs key to allow the partner's account, then modify the snapshot permissions to add that account
options.explanation: The key policy of an AWS managed key cannot be edited, so the partner can never be granted use of it.

options.text: Copy the snapshot into an unencrypted snapshot, share that copy with the partner, and have the partner copy it with its own key
options.explanation: A copy of an encrypted snapshot cannot be decrypted into plaintext, and the requirements forbid unencrypted data anyway.

options.text: Copy the snapshot re-encrypted with a customer managed KMS key, allow the partner in that key's policy, and share the copy

explanation: Sharing an encrypted snapshot also requires sharing the KMS key that encrypts it. AWS managed keys cannot be shared, so the snapshot is copied and re-encrypted under a customer managed key, the key policy grants the partner account use of the key, and the copy's permissions add the partner, who can then copy it under its own key. An unencrypted copy is neither possible nor allowed. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/ebs/latest/userguide/ebs-modifying-snapshot-permissions.html

prompt:
A startup has just created its first AWS account. The founder signs in with the email address and password used at sign-up and has created access keys for that identity so that a deployment script can run. The company wants to protect the account's root user the way AWS recommends.

Which solution meets this requirement?

options.text: Keep the root access keys but store them in AWS Secrets Manager with scheduled rotation, and enable MFA on the root user
options.explanation: The root user should have no access keys at all; keeping them in a secret still leaves long-term credentials with unrestricted access to the account.

options.text: Delete the root access keys, enable root MFA, run the script with an IAM role, and keep root for tasks that need it
Attach a restrictive IAM policy to the root user that limits it to the deployment actions the script needs to perform
options.explanation: IAM policies can't be attached to the root user, so its permissions in a standalone account can't be narrowed this way.

options.text: Enable MFA on the root user and rotate its access keys every 90 days, with an AWS Config rule that flags keys older than that
options.explanation: Rotation shortens each key's life, but the root user still holds long-term keys with unrestricted access, which AWS advises against.

explanation: AWS recommends that the root user has no access keys, is protected with MFA, and is used only for the few tasks that require root credentials; everyday work, including automation, runs as IAM roles with temporary credentials. Storing or rotating root keys still leaves unrestricted long-term credentials in place, and IAM policies can't be attached to the root user to narrow what it can do. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/root-user-best-practices.html

prompt:
A company has 25 data analysts, each with an IAM user. Today every analyst's user has its own inline policy granting the same Amazon Athena and Amazon S3 read permissions, and analysts join and leave the team every month. The security team wants to change the analysts' permissions in one place and to grant or remove access only by changing team membership.

Which solution meets these requirements?

options.text: Copy the inline policy into a customer managed policy and attach that managed policy to each analyst's IAM user
options.explanation: A shared managed policy gives one place to edit, but access is still granted user by user rather than through team membership.

options.text: Create an IAM role with the analyst permissions and add each analyst's IAM user to the role's list of members
options.explanation: IAM roles have no member list; users assume a role through its trust policy, so a role does not collect users the way a group does.

options.text: Create a permissions boundary that allows the Athena and S3 read actions and set it on each analyst's IAM user
options.explanation: A permissions boundary only caps permissions and grants none, and it is still set on each user individually.

options.text: Create an IAM group with a managed policy for the Athena and S3 read access, and add each analyst's IAM user to it

explanation: An IAM group holds the permissions once: every IAM user in the group gets the group's policies, editing the group's policy changes access for the whole team, and adding or removing a user from the group is the only step when analysts join or leave. A managed policy attached per user still grants access user by user, roles have no members, and a permissions boundary grants nothing on its own. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/id_groups.html

prompt:
An application on Amazon EC2 instances sends messages to an Amazon SQS queue in the same account. A developer placed an IAM user's access key ID and secret access key in the application's configuration file. A security review requires that no long-term credentials be stored on the instances and that the application's credentials be rotated automatically.

Which solution meets these requirements?

options.text: Create an IAM role that allows sqs:SendMessage on the queue, attach it through an instance profile, and remove the keys
Move the access keys into AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store as a SecureString parameter that the application reads at startup
options.explanation: The keys are still an IAM user's long-term credentials; the parameter changes where they are kept but does not rotate them.

options.text: Rotate the IAM user's access keys every 30 days with an AWS Lambda function and push new keys to the instances with Run Command
options.explanation: This automates rotation, but long-term IAM user keys still sit on the instances, which the review forbids.

options.text: Use IAM Roles Anywhere to issue the instances temporary credentials based on an X.509 certificate installed on each instance
options.explanation: IAM Roles Anywhere is for workloads outside AWS; EC2 instances get temporary credentials from an instance profile without any certificates to manage.

explanation: An IAM role attached through an instance profile gives the application temporary credentials from the instance metadata service; the AWS SDK picks them up, and they are rotated automatically before they expire, so no keys are stored on the instance. Parameter Store and a rotation function both keep long-term IAM user keys in play, and IAM Roles Anywhere targets servers outside AWS. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/id_roles_use_switch-role-ec2.html

prompt:
A company is moving a web application to Amazon EC2 instances that run Amazon Linux and its MySQL database to Amazon RDS for MySQL. The compliance team must record who is responsible for operating system security patches on each part of the new architecture.

Which statement is correct?

options.text: AWS patches the operating systems of both the EC2 instances and the RDS DB instances, because both run on hardware that AWS manages
options.explanation: AWS secures the hosts and virtualization layer, but the guest operating system on an EC2 instance is the customer's to patch.

options.text: The company patches the operating systems of both the EC2 instances and the RDS DB instances by using AWS Systems Manager Patch Manager
options.explanation: Amazon RDS gives no operating system access; RDS supplies the OS updates for DB instances and installs them in the maintenance window.

options.text: The company patches the EC2 guest OS; Amazon RDS supplies and applies OS updates to the DB instances in a chosen window
AWS patches the EC2 guest OS because the instances use an AWS-provided AMI, and the company patches the RDS OS through DB parameter groups
options.explanation: Launching from an AWS-provided AMI does not hand guest OS patching to AWS, and parameter groups set engine options, not OS patches.

explanation: Under the shared responsibility model, the customer manages the guest operating system of an EC2 instance, including updates and security patches. Amazon RDS is a managed service: RDS supplies operating system updates for DB instances and applies them during the maintenance window the company chooses, and customers have no OS access to patch. Neither the AMI's publisher nor the hardware owner takes over EC2 guest patching. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSEC2/latest/UserGuide/ec2-security.html

prompt:
A company is about to grow from one AWS account to about 20 accounts for separate teams and environments. From day one it wants a multi-account environment that follows AWS best practices: a central log archive account and audit account, preventive and detective guardrails on every new account, and a self-service way to create accounts that comply with those guardrails.

Which solution meets these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

options.text: Set up a landing zone with AWS Control Tower and create new accounts through its Account Factory so that the enabled controls apply to them
Create an organization in AWS Organizations, write SCPs and AWS Config rules for each guardrail, and create accounts with the CreateAccount API
options.explanation: This can reach the same result, but the team must build and maintain the log accounts, guardrails, and account vending itself.

options.text: Publish an account template product in AWS Service Catalog that teams launch to create accounts, with AWS Config turned on in each
options.explanation: Service Catalog distributes products, but on its own it does not set up a log archive, an audit account, or preventive guardrails.

options.text: Create an organization with IAM Identity Center for sign-in and deploy a set of AWS Config conformance packs to every account
options.explanation: Conformance packs only detect noncompliance, and this setup gives no shared log archive or audit account and no governed account vending.

explanation: AWS Control Tower sets up a governed landing zone on AWS Organizations: it creates the log archive and audit accounts, applies preventive and detective controls to the OUs, and its Account Factory lets teams create new accounts that inherit those controls. Building the same pieces from SCPs, Config rules, and scripts works but carries far more overhead, while Service Catalog alone or conformance packs alone cover only part of the requirement. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/controltower/latest/userguide/what-is-control-tower.html

prompt:
A company runs 40 accounts in AWS Organizations. The security team needs a continuously updated list of the Amazon S3 buckets, IAM roles, AWS KMS keys, and Amazon SQS queues whose resource-based policies grant access to principals outside the organization, so that it can review each case.

Which solution meets this requirement with the LEAST operational overhead?

options.text: Turn on Amazon GuardDuty for the organization and review its findings for resources that are shared with other accounts
options.explanation: GuardDuty looks for suspicious activity in logs; it does not analyze role trust, key, and queue policies for external principals.

options.text: Turn on Amazon Macie for the organization and use its bucket inventory to report resources shared with other accounts
options.explanation: Macie reports whether S3 buckets are shared or public, but it covers S3 only, not IAM roles, KMS keys, or SQS queues.

options.text: Write an AWS Config custom rule for each account that parses resource policies and flags principals from other account IDs
options.explanation: Custom parsing must be built and maintained for each resource type and easily misses the conditions and wildcards that grant outside access.

options.text: Create an IAM Access Analyzer external access analyzer with the organization as its zone of trust in each Region in use

explanation: An IAM Access Analyzer external access analyzer with the organization as its zone of trust analyzes the resource-based policies of supported resources, including S3 buckets, IAM roles, KMS keys, and SQS queues, and creates a finding for each one shared with a principal outside the organization; it re-analyzes policies as they change. GuardDuty and Macie answer different questions, and custom Config rules mean writing your own policy analysis. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/what-is-access-analyzer.html

prompt:
A developer's IAM user belongs to two IAM groups. The Developers group has a policy that allows all Amazon EC2 actions on all resources. The Guardrails group has a policy that denies ec2:TerminateInstances on instances tagged env=prod. The developer tries to terminate an instance tagged env=prod.

What is the result of the request?

options.text: The request is allowed because the Developers group policy was attached first and is evaluated before the Guardrails policy
options.explanation: IAM does not evaluate policies in attachment order; it gathers all applicable policies before it reaches a decision.

options.text: The request is allowed because the Developers group's EC2 allow is broader than the deny, which names a single action
options.explanation: How broad a statement is does not matter; a matching explicit deny overrides any allow.

options.text: The request is denied because an explicit deny in any applicable policy overrides an allow in any other policy
The request is denied only if the developer's IAM user also has a permissions boundary that omits ec2:TerminateInstances
options.explanation: No boundary is needed; the explicit deny in the Guardrails group policy is enough on its own to block the action.

explanation: IAM evaluates all policies that apply to the request together. An explicit deny in any of them overrides every allow, so the Guardrails group's deny on ec2:TerminateInstances for env=prod instances wins over the Developers group's allow for all EC2 actions. Attachment order and how broad an allow is play no part, and no permissions boundary is required for the deny to take effect. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/reference_policies_evaluation-logic.html

prompt:
A company has a development account and a production account. Members of the Ops IAM group sign in to the AWS Management Console in the development account. They must be able to view resources in the production account through the console with read-only access, without IAM users or passwords in the production account. No other users in the development account may get this access.

Which combination of steps meets these requirements? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Create a read-only IAM user in the production account for each Ops member and require MFA for console sign-in
options.explanation: Separate IAM users with passwords in production are exactly what the company wants to avoid.

options.text: In the production account, create a role with the ReadOnlyAccess policy whose trust policy names the development account
Share the production account's resources with the development account by using AWS Resource Access Manager
options.explanation: AWS RAM shares specific resource types such as subnets; it does not give console users read-only access to another account.

options.text: Add resource-based policies in the production account that name the development account's Ops IAM group as principal
options.explanation: An IAM group can't be a principal in a resource-based policy, and many services have no resource-based policies at all.

options.text: Give the Ops group in the development account a policy that allows sts:AssumeRole on that role, then use Switch Role

explanation: Cross-account console access is a role in the production account whose trust policy names the development account, plus a policy in the development account that allows sts:AssumeRole on that role. Granting sts:AssumeRole only to the Ops group keeps everyone else out, and Switch Role in the console gives temporary credentials with no production users or passwords. RAM shares specific resources, not console access, and IAM groups can't be named as principals. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/id_roles_use_switch-role-console.html

prompt:
A company runs 60 projects in one AWS account, and new projects start every week. Each developer signs in through IAM Identity Center, and the developer's project attribute is passed into the session as a principal tag named project. Every Amazon EC2 instance carries a project tag. Developers must be able to start, stop, and reboot only the instances of their own project, and the security team wants no policy edits when a project is added.

Which solution meets these requirements?

options.text: Allow the EC2 actions in one policy with a condition that aws:ResourceTag/project equals ${aws:PrincipalTag/project}
Create a permission set per project whose policy lists that project's instance ARNs in the Resource element
options.explanation: Listing ARNs works for today's projects, but every new project and instance needs a new permission set or a policy edit.

options.text: Put each project's instances in its own VPC and allow the EC2 actions with an ec2:Vpc condition for each project
options.explanation: Every new project needs a new VPC and a new policy condition, which the security team wants to avoid.

options.text: Allow the EC2 actions in one policy with a condition that aws:RequestTag/project equals each project's name
options.explanation: aws:RequestTag checks tags sent in the request, not tags already on the instance, and fixed names mean editing the policy per project.

explanation: Attribute-based access control compares a tag on the principal with a tag on the resource. A single policy that allows the actions when aws:ResourceTag/project equals ${aws:PrincipalTag/project} lets each developer manage only matching instances and needs no change when a new project starts, as long as instances are tagged. Per-project ARNs or VPCs need policy edits for every project, and aws:RequestTag describes tags in the request, not the instance's tags. To keep it safe, also stop developers from changing project tags. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/introduction_attribute-based-access-control.html

prompt:
A company wants a third-party cost-monitoring SaaS provider to read billing and Amazon CloudWatch data in the company's AWS account. The provider runs its service for many customers from its own AWS account. The company will create no long-term credentials for the provider and must prevent another customer of the provider from getting the provider to access the company's account on that customer's behalf.

Which solution meets these requirements?

options.text: Create an IAM user with read permissions for the provider and share its access keys with the provider through AWS Secrets Manager
options.explanation: IAM user access keys are long-term credentials, which the company must not create for the provider.

options.text: Create an IAM role that trusts the provider's AWS account and grants read access, and require MFA in the role's trust policy
options.explanation: MFA blocks the provider's automated calls, and trusting the account alone does nothing to stop the confused deputy problem.

options.text: Create an IAM role that trusts the provider's AWS account, and restrict it with aws:SourceIp to the provider's published IP ranges
options.explanation: Requests made for other customers come from the same provider systems and addresses, so the IP condition can't tell them apart.

options.text: Create an IAM role that trusts the provider's account and requires the unique external ID the provider gave the company

explanation: A role gives the provider temporary credentials through AWS STS, so no long-term keys exist. Because one provider account acts for many customers, the trust policy should also require an sts:ExternalId value that the provider generates uniquely for this company; another customer can't make the provider present this company's external ID, which closes the confused deputy gap. An IP or MFA condition doesn't separate one customer's requests from another's. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/id_roles_common-scenarios_third-party.html

prompt:
A company in AWS Organizations must keep all workloads in eu-west-1 and eu-central-1 for data residency. Administrators in member accounts must still be able to manage IAM, Amazon CloudFront, Amazon Route 53, and AWS Support, whose requests are handled in us-east-1. The control must apply to every member account, and account administrators must be unable to remove it.

Which solution meets these requirements?

options.text: Attach an SCP to the organization root that denies any action when aws:RequestedRegion is outside the two Regions
options.explanation: With no exemption for global services, requests to IAM, CloudFront, Route 53, and Support resolve to us-east-1 and are denied.

options.text: Disable the other Regions in each member account's Region settings so that just the two approved Regions stay enabled
options.explanation: Only opt-in Regions can be disabled; Regions enabled by default, such as us-east-1, stay available.

options.text: Attach an SCP that denies any request outside the two Regions, using NotAction to exempt those global services
Attach an IAM policy with the Region deny and the global service exemption to the users and roles in each member account
options.explanation: Account administrators can detach or edit IAM policies in their own account, so they could remove the control.

explanation: An SCP binds every principal in the member accounts, and their administrators can't detach it. A Deny with NotAction for the global services and a StringNotEquals condition on aws:RequestedRegion blocks requests outside the approved Regions while leaving IAM, CloudFront, Route 53, and Support working, because those services take requests in us-east-1. The same deny without NotAction breaks those services, default Regions can't be disabled, and IAM policies can be removed by account administrators. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/reference_policies_examples_aws_deny-requested-region.html

prompt:
Users of a mobile app sign in through an Amazon Cognito user pool and upload photos from their devices straight to an Amazon S3 bucket. Each user must be able to read and write only objects under their own prefix in the bucket. The app must contain no AWS credentials, and uploads must go straight to S3 with no backend server in the path.

Which solution meets these requirements?

options.text: Have the app send each photo to an Amazon API Gateway API whose Lambda function writes it to S3 under the user's prefix
options.explanation: API Gateway and Lambda put a backend in the upload path, which the requirements rule out.

options.text: Use a Cognito identity pool whose authenticated role allows S3 access under the prefix ${cognito-identity.amazonaws.com:sub}
Send the user pool ID token with each S3 request and add a bucket policy that maps the token's sub claim to the prefix
options.explanation: S3 does not accept user pool tokens as request credentials; they must first be exchanged for AWS credentials through an identity pool.

options.text: Create one IAM user for the app, ship its keys in the app build, and limit each request to a prefix of ${aws:username}
options.explanation: Every install shares long-term keys, and aws:username is that single IAM user's name, not the person using the app.

explanation: A Cognito identity pool exchanges the user pool token for temporary AWS credentials of the authenticated role, so the app holds no stored credentials and talks to S3 directly. The policy variable ${cognito-identity.amazonaws.com:sub} resolves to each user's identity ID, so one role policy confines every user to their own prefix. S3 can't read user pool tokens itself, an API backend is ruled out, and shared IAM user keys are both stored and identical for every user. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/cognito/latest/developerguide/iam-roles.html

prompt:
A company has 120 accounts in AWS Organizations and adds new accounts every month. No Amazon S3 bucket in any account may be made public, including buckets in accounts created later. Account administrators must be unable to turn the protection off, and the security team wants to configure it once for the whole organization.

Which solution meets these requirements?

options.text: Turn on all four account-level S3 Block Public Access settings in every member account by using a CloudFormation StackSet
options.explanation: Account administrators can still edit their own account-level Block Public Access settings and switch the protection off.

options.text: Deploy the AWS Config rule s3-bucket-level-public-access-prohibited everywhere with remediation that turns the settings back on
options.explanation: AWS Config acts after the change, so a bucket can be public until the remediation runs.

options.text: Attach an Amazon S3 policy in AWS Organizations to the organization root that turns on all four Block Public Access settings
Rely on the Block Public Access settings that S3 turns on for each new bucket, and track any changes with AWS CloudTrail
options.explanation: Bucket owners can turn the default bucket-level settings off, and CloudTrail records that change rather than preventing it.

explanation: An Amazon S3 policy in AWS Organizations sets all four Block Public Access settings for every account it covers, overrides the account-level configuration, stops account administrators from changing it while it is attached, and is inherited by accounts that join later. Account-level settings pushed by StackSets can be changed by administrators, AWS Config only repairs after the fact, and default bucket settings can be switched off by bucket owners. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/organizations/latest/userguide/orgs_manage_policies_s3.html

prompt:
An IAM role named Analytics in account A must read objects from an Amazon S3 bucket in account B. The role's identity-based policy allows s3:GetObject on the bucket's objects, and the bucket policy in account B allows s3:GetObject for the Analytics role ARN. The objects use SSE-S3, Object Ownership is set to bucket owner enforced, and neither policy contains a Deny. Both accounts are in the same organization. Account A is in an OU whose only SCP allows Amazon EC2, Amazon DynamoDB, and CloudWatch Logs actions; FullAWSAccess is detached from that OU. Every call returns AccessDenied.

What is the cause of the error?

options.text: A bucket policy can grant cross-account access only to a whole account, so its principal must be account A's root ARN
options.explanation: A bucket policy can name an individual role in another account; the role ARN is a valid cross-account principal.

options.text: The SCP on account A's OU does not allow s3:GetObject, so account A's evaluation ends in an implicit deny
Account B also needs a resource control policy that allows account A, because a bucket policy alone can't grant access
options.explanation: RCPs only restrict access to resources and never grant it; the bucket policy is what grants the cross-account access.

options.text: The role must assume a role in account B first, because account A identity policies are ignored for account B resources
options.explanation: Account A's identity policy is evaluated and counts; a role can call the bucket directly when both accounts' policies allow it.

explanation: A cross-account request is evaluated in both accounts and succeeds only if both evaluations allow it. Account A's evaluation includes the SCPs that limit its principals, and an allow-list SCP that omits S3 leaves s3:GetObject implicitly denied, whatever the identity policy and the bucket policy grant. Role ARNs are valid bucket policy principals, RCPs never grant access, and account A's identity policy is part of the decision rather than ignored. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/reference_policies_evaluation-logic-cross-account.html

prompt:
A shared-services account hosts an Amazon S3 bucket of approved software installers. Every IAM principal in the company's organization (o-a1b2c3d4e5), including principals in accounts added later, must be able to download the objects, and principals outside the organization must be refused. The bucket policy must need no edits when accounts join or leave. IAM policies in the member accounts already allow s3:GetObject on the bucket.

Which bucket policy statement meets these requirements?

options.text: Allow s3:GetObject with the member account IDs as principals, and update the list from an EventBridge rule on CreateAccount events
options.explanation: Listing account IDs means the policy is rewritten whenever an account joins or leaves, even if the update is automated.

options.text: Allow s3:GetObject to all principals with a condition that aws:SourceOrgID equals o-a1b2c3d4e5
options.explanation: aws:SourceOrgID describes the resource behind an AWS service calling on your behalf, so it is absent when IAM principals call S3 directly.

options.text: Allow s3:GetObject to all principals with a condition that aws:PrincipalOrgPaths matches the path of the Workloads OU
options.explanation: Only principals in accounts under that OU match, so accounts elsewhere in the organization are left out.

options.text: Allow s3:GetObject to all principals with a condition that aws:PrincipalOrgID equals o-a1b2c3d4e5

explanation: aws:PrincipalOrgID compares the organization of the calling principal with the value in the policy, so a statement that allows all principals on this condition admits every account in the organization, picks up new accounts automatically, and needs no edits as accounts come and go; principals outside the organization don't match. aws:SourceOrgID is meant for AWS service principals acting for a resource, an OU path admits only part of the organization, and an account list must be maintained. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/reference_policies_condition-keys.html#condition-keys-principalorgid

prompt:
A company attached an SCP to the root of its organization that denies iam:CreateUser and iam:CreateAccessKey, so that all access uses roles. A month later an audit finds new IAM users with access keys in the management account, created by an administrator there. No member account has any new IAM users. The security team asks why the SCP failed to stop this and what to change.

Which response is correct?

options.text: SCPs don't affect the management account; move workloads into member accounts and tightly limit who can use it
SCPs attached to the root are inherited only by OUs; attach the same SCP directly to the management account as well
options.explanation: SCPs have no effect on the management account wherever they are attached, and root SCPs do apply to accounts directly under the root.

options.text: SCPs restrict roles but not IAM users; recreate the deny as a resource control policy, which also covers IAM users
options.explanation: SCPs restrict IAM users and roles in member accounts alike; the gap is the management account, and RCPs don't govern IAM user creation.

options.text: The administrator had AdministratorAccess, which overrides SCPs; set a permissions boundary on the account's administrators
options.explanation: AdministratorAccess doesn't override an SCP in a member account, and administrators who manage IAM can remove a boundary.

explanation: SCPs affect only member accounts; they never restrict users or roles in the management account, wherever the SCP is attached. AWS therefore recommends keeping workloads out of the management account and limiting access to it, so the guardrails apply where work happens. Root-attached SCPs do reach every member account, SCPs restrict IAM users as well as roles, and RCPs don't cover IAM user creation. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/organizations/latest/userguide/orgs_manage_policies_scps.html

prompt:
An application role in account B (222222222222) must call kms:Decrypt on a symmetric customer managed key in account A (111111111111) to decrypt data keys that arrive with the records it processes. Account A's security team wants to decide which accounts may use the key. Account B's team wants to decide which of its own roles get that access.

Which combination of steps meets these requirements? (Select TWO.)

options.text: In account A, add a key policy statement allowing arn:aws:iam::222222222222:root kms:Decrypt and kms:DescribeKey
In account A, use AWS Resource Access Manager to share the customer managed key with account B
options.explanation: AWS RAM does not share KMS keys; cross-account use of a key is granted in its key policy.

options.text: In account A, create a multi-Region replica of the key and place the replica key in account B
options.explanation: Multi-Region replica keys stay in the same account as the primary key and differ only in Region.

options.text: In account B, attach an IAM policy to the application role allowing kms:Decrypt on account A's key ARN
In account B, create an alias that points to the key in account A and allow the role kms:Decrypt on the alias
options.explanation: An alias can only point to a KMS key in its own account and Region, so it can't refer to account A's key.

explanation: Cross-account use of a KMS key needs two policies. The key policy in account A must allow account B, which is how account A decides which accounts may use the key, and an IAM policy in account B must delegate that permission to specific roles by naming the key ARN, which is how account B chooses its roles. Neither alone is enough. RAM can't share KMS keys, multi-Region replicas stay in the owning account, and aliases can't point across accounts. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/kms/latest/developerguide/key-policy-modifying-external-accounts.html

prompt:
Amazon EC2 instances in private subnets must download operating system patches from repositories on the internet. The instances must stay unreachable from the internet, they use IPv4 only, and the operations team wants a managed service rather than another server to patch and scale.

Which solution meets these requirements?

options.text: Add a route from the private subnets to the internet gateway and assign each instance a public IPv4 address for its downloads
options.explanation: An internet gateway route plus a public IP makes each instance reachable from the internet, so the subnets are no longer private.

options.text: Create a NAT gateway in a public subnet and point the private subnets' default route at the NAT gateway
Attach an egress-only internet gateway to the VPC and point the private subnets' default route at it
options.explanation: An egress-only internet gateway handles outbound IPv6 traffic only; these instances use IPv4.

options.text: Launch a NAT instance from a NAT AMI in a public subnet and point the private subnets' default route at it
options.explanation: A NAT instance works, but it is an EC2 server the team must patch, size and make highly available itself.

explanation: A public NAT gateway in a public subnet lets instances in private subnets start connections to the internet, while nothing on the internet can start a connection back to them; AWS manages and scales it. A route to the internet gateway with public IPs exposes the instances, an egress-only internet gateway is for IPv6 only, and a NAT instance is a server the team would have to run. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/vpc/latest/userguide/vpc-nat-gateway.html

prompt:
Administrators need interactive shell access to Linux instances in private subnets. The security team wants inbound port 22 closed on every instance, no bastion hosts or SSH keys to manage, and a record of the commands each administrator runs stored in Amazon S3.

Which solution meets these requirements?

options.text: Deploy a bastion host in a public subnet whose security group allows SSH only from the office IP range, and log its sessions
options.explanation: A bastion host is exactly the server the team wants to avoid, and the instances still need port 22 open to it.

options.text: Create an EC2 Instance Connect Endpoint in the VPC and allow SSH to the instances from the endpoint's security group
options.explanation: Instance Connect Endpoint removes the bastion but still needs port 22 open to the instances and does not log commands to S3.

options.text: Set up AWS Client VPN for the administrators and allow SSH to the instances from the Client VPN endpoint's subnets
options.explanation: Client VPN gives network access, but administrators still use SSH keys over an open port 22 and no command log is kept.

options.text: Use AWS Systems Manager Session Manager with the SSM Agent and an instance profile, and send session logs to S3

explanation: Session Manager opens shell sessions through the SSM Agent's outbound connection to Systems Manager, so instances need no open inbound ports, no bastion and no SSH keys, and IAM policies control who may connect; session activity can be logged to S3 or CloudWatch Logs. A bastion, an Instance Connect Endpoint and Client VPN all still rely on SSH over port 22. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/systems-manager/latest/userguide/session-manager.html

prompt:
A company serves a web application through an internet-facing Application Load Balancer. For legal reasons, requests that originate from two specific countries must be blocked; traffic from everywhere else must continue to reach the application. The company wants to avoid adding another service in front of the load balancer.

Which solution meets these requirements?

options.text: Associate an AWS WAF web ACL with the load balancer that has a geographic match rule blocking the two countries
Add deny rules to the load balancer subnets' network ACLs for the published IP ranges of the two countries
options.explanation: Country IP ranges are large and change often, and network ACLs hold a limited number of rules, so this cannot be kept accurate.

options.text: Configure Amazon Route 53 geolocation routing so that queries from the two countries receive no answer for the domain
options.explanation: Geolocation routing shapes DNS answers only; clients that already know the load balancer's address still reach it.

options.text: Put an Amazon CloudFront distribution in front of the load balancer and turn on its geographic restriction feature
options.explanation: CloudFront geo restriction can block countries, but it adds a new service in front of the load balancer, which the company wants to avoid.

explanation: An AWS WAF geo match statement identifies each request's country of origin from its IP address, and a rule with the Block action stops requests from the listed countries at the load balancer itself. Network ACLs cannot track country ranges, Route 53 geolocation only changes DNS answers, and CloudFront geo restriction means adding a distribution in front of the load balancer. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/waf/latest/developerguide/waf-rule-statement-type-geo-match.html

prompt:
A company runs workloads on Amazon EC2 instances, container images stored in Amazon ECR, and AWS Lambda functions. The security team must find known software vulnerabilities (CVEs) in these workloads and have them re-evaluated automatically when a new CVE is published, without scheduling scans.

Which AWS service meets these requirements?

options.text: Amazon GuardDuty with Runtime Monitoring turned on for the EC2 instances and the container workloads
options.explanation: GuardDuty detects threats and suspicious behavior from logs and runtime events; it does not inventory packages for known CVEs.

options.text: AWS Security Hub CSPM with the AWS Foundational Security Best Practices standard enabled
options.explanation: Security Hub CSPM checks resource configuration and aggregates findings from other services; it does not scan software for CVEs itself.

options.text: Amazon Inspector activated for EC2, Amazon ECR and Lambda scanning in the account
AWS Config with managed rules that evaluate the EC2 instances, ECR repositories and Lambda functions
options.explanation: AWS Config evaluates resource configuration against rules; it has no vulnerability database to match installed packages against.

explanation: Amazon Inspector automatically discovers EC2 instances, ECR container images and Lambda functions, scans them for software vulnerabilities and unintended network exposure, and rescans when a new CVE affecting a resource is published. GuardDuty looks for threats in activity, Security Hub CSPM runs configuration checks and collects findings, and AWS Config evaluates configuration, so none of them finds vulnerable packages. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/inspector/latest/user/what-is-inspector.html

prompt:
A company has 25 AWS accounts in AWS Organizations across three Regions, with Amazon GuardDuty, Amazon Inspector and Amazon Macie enabled. The security team wants one place to see and prioritize the findings from these services for every account and Region, and to check the accounts against the AWS Foundational Security Best Practices standard.

Which solution meets these requirements?

options.text: Enable Amazon Detective in a delegated administrator account and add each member account to its behavior graph
options.explanation: Detective helps investigate the root cause of a finding; it does not aggregate findings or run best-practice checks.

options.text: Enable AWS Security Hub CSPM with a delegated administrator account and turn on cross-Region aggregation
Create an organization trail in AWS CloudTrail that delivers to a central S3 bucket and query it with Amazon Athena
options.explanation: CloudTrail records API activity, not the findings that GuardDuty, Inspector and Macie produce, and it runs no standard checks.

options.text: Create an AWS Config aggregator in a central account that collects configuration data from each account and Region
options.explanation: A Config aggregator collects configuration and rule compliance, not the findings from GuardDuty, Inspector and Macie.

explanation: Security Hub CSPM receives findings from GuardDuty, Inspector, Macie and partner products in a standard format, consolidates them across the organization's accounts through a delegated administrator, can aggregate them into one Region, and runs controls from standards such as AWS Foundational Security Best Practices. Detective investigates, CloudTrail records API calls, and a Config aggregator collects configuration data only. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/securityhub/latest/userguide/what-is-securityhub.html

prompt:
About 200 employees work from home on company laptops. They need encrypted access to internal web applications that run in private subnets of a VPC. The applications must stay unreachable from the public internet, and the company wants a managed service that scales with the number of users.

Which solution meets these requirements?

options.text: Create an AWS Site-to-Site VPN connection to the VPC's virtual private gateway for the employees to connect through
options.explanation: Site-to-Site VPN links a network with a customer gateway device to the VPC; it is not a client service for individual laptops.

options.text: Order an AWS Direct Connect hosted connection and create a private virtual interface to the VPC for the employees
options.explanation: Direct Connect is a physical link from a data center or colocation site; home laptops cannot use it, and it is unencrypted by default.

options.text: Place the applications behind an internet-facing Application Load Balancer with an HTTPS listener and an ACM certificate
options.explanation: TLS encrypts the traffic, but an internet-facing load balancer makes the applications reachable from the public internet.

options.text: Create an AWS Client VPN endpoint associated with the VPC subnets and have the employees connect with a VPN client

explanation: AWS Client VPN is a managed, client-based VPN: each employee's OpenVPN-based client opens an encrypted TLS tunnel to the Client VPN endpoint, which scales with the number of users and reaches the private subnets without exposing them. Site-to-Site VPN connects networks rather than laptops, Direct Connect is a physical circuit, and a public load balancer exposes the applications. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/vpn/latest/clientvpn-admin/what-is.html

prompt:
Web servers on Amazon EC2 run in a public subnet without a load balancer. The subnet's network ACL has inbound rule 100 that allows TCP 443 from 0.0.0.0/0. Monitoring shows abusive requests coming from the range 198.51.100.0/24. The team must stop all traffic from that range at the subnet while every other client keeps access.

Which solution meets these requirements?

options.text: Add an inbound network ACL rule numbered 90 that denies all traffic from 198.51.100.0/24
Add an inbound rule to the web servers' security group that denies all traffic from 198.51.100.0/24
options.explanation: Security groups support allow rules only, so there is no deny rule to add.

options.text: Add an inbound network ACL rule numbered 110 that denies all traffic from 198.51.100.0/24
options.explanation: Network ACL rules are evaluated lowest number first; HTTPS from the range matches the allow in rule 100 before rule 110 is reached.

options.text: Create an AWS WAF web ACL with an IP set rule that blocks 198.51.100.0/24 and associate it with the instances
options.explanation: AWS WAF attaches to resources such as load balancers, API Gateway and CloudFront, not directly to EC2 instances.

explanation: Network ACLs support deny rules and evaluate them in order from the lowest rule number, stopping at the first match, so a deny numbered below the HTTPS allow blocks the range before it can match rule 100. Security groups have no deny rules, a deny numbered after the allow is never reached for HTTPS, and AWS WAF cannot be associated with an EC2 instance. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/vpc/latest/userguide/vpc-network-acls.html

prompt:
Web servers in a public subnet use a custom network ACL with one inbound rule that allows TCP 443 from 0.0.0.0/0 and one outbound rule that allows TCP 443 to 0.0.0.0/0. Users' HTTPS requests to the servers time out, and the servers' own HTTPS calls to an external payment API also time out. The security groups allow the traffic. The team wants to keep a custom network ACL rather than switch to one that allows all traffic.

Which TWO changes together fix both problems? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Add an outbound rule to the web servers' security group that allows TCP 1024-65535 to 0.0.0.0/0
options.explanation: Security groups are stateful and already allow responses; the stateless network ACL is still dropping the packets.

options.text: Add an outbound network ACL rule that allows TCP 1024-65535 to 0.0.0.0/0
Add an inbound network ACL rule that allows TCP 443 from 0.0.0.0/0 with a lower rule number
options.explanation: Inbound 443 is already allowed; renumbering it changes nothing because the missing rules are for return traffic.

options.text: Associate the subnet with the VPC's default network ACL in place of the custom network ACL
options.explanation: The default network ACL allows all inbound and outbound traffic, which the team has ruled out.

options.text: Add an inbound network ACL rule that allows TCP 1024-65535 from 0.0.0.0/0

explanation: Network ACLs are stateless, so return traffic needs its own rule. Responses to users leave the subnet toward the clients' ephemeral ports, which needs an outbound allow for 1024-65535; responses from the payment API come back to the servers' ephemeral ports, which needs an inbound allow for the same range. A security group rule cannot fix a network ACL drop, inbound 443 is already allowed, and the default network ACL allows all traffic. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/vpc/latest/userguide/custom-network-acl.html

prompt:
A company runs a customer portal on Amazon EC2 instances behind an Application Load Balancer. Customers must sign in with either their Google account or the company's SAML identity provider before any request reaches the instances. The developers want to keep authentication code out of the application entirely.

Which solution meets these requirements with the LEAST development effort?

options.text: Create an Amazon Cognito identity pool that federates Google and the SAML provider and returns AWS credentials to the portal
options.explanation: Identity pools issue AWS credentials to an app that has already signed users in; they do not gate requests at the load balancer.

options.text: Configure IAM Identity Center with the SAML provider as its identity source and assign the portal as a customer managed application
options.explanation: IAM Identity Center serves the workforce; it does not federate customers' Google accounts or put a sign-in step in front of the ALB.

options.text: Create a Cognito user pool that federates Google and the SAML provider, and add an authenticate-cognito action to the HTTPS listener
Create a Cognito user pool that federates Google and the SAML provider, and add an authenticate-cognito action to the HTTP listener on port 80
options.explanation: The ALB authenticate actions are supported only on HTTPS listeners, so this rule cannot be created on an HTTP listener.

explanation: An Application Load Balancer can authenticate users itself: a listener rule with an authenticate-cognito action redirects unauthenticated users to a Cognito user pool, which can federate social and SAML identity providers, and only then forwards the request with the user's claims. Authenticate actions work only on HTTPS listeners, identity pools hand out AWS credentials rather than gate requests, and IAM Identity Center does not federate customer social logins. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/elasticloadbalancing/latest/application/listener-authenticate-users.html

prompt:
AWS Lambda functions attached to private subnets call AWS Secrets Manager through the AWS SDK using its default endpoint, and the calls time out. The VPC has no internet gateway or NAT gateway, and the security team forbids adding any path to the internet. The function code and SDK configuration must stay unchanged.

Which solution meets these requirements?

options.text: Create an interface VPC endpoint for Secrets Manager with private DNS enabled, and allow HTTPS to it from the functions' security group
Create a gateway VPC endpoint for Secrets Manager and add it to the route tables associated with the functions' private subnets
options.explanation: Gateway endpoints exist for Amazon S3 and DynamoDB only; Secrets Manager is reached through an interface endpoint.

options.text: Create an interface VPC endpoint for Secrets Manager with private DNS disabled, and allow HTTPS to it from the functions' security group
options.explanation: Without private DNS the default Secrets Manager hostname still resolves to public addresses, so the SDK would need the endpoint's DNS name.

options.text: Add a NAT gateway in a new public subnet and route the functions' private subnets to it for traffic bound for Secrets Manager
options.explanation: A NAT gateway needs an internet gateway, which adds the internet path the security team forbids.

explanation: An interface VPC endpoint places network interfaces for Secrets Manager in the subnets, and with private DNS enabled (and DNS hostnames and resolution on in the VPC) the service's default hostname resolves to those private IPs, so unchanged SDK calls stay inside the VPC. Gateway endpoints exist only for S3 and DynamoDB, disabling private DNS forces a code change, and a NAT gateway needs an internet path. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/vpc/latest/privatelink/privatelink-access-aws-services.html

prompt:
An online retailer serves its site through Amazon CloudFront, an Application Load Balancer and an Amazon Route 53 hosted zone. A past DDoS attack forced heavy scaling and a large bill. The company, which has an AWS Business Support plan, now wants access to AWS DDoS experts during an attack and a way to recover charges caused by attack-driven scaling.

Which solution meets these requirements?

options.text: Rely on AWS Shield Standard, which is active on CloudFront and Route 53, and open a Business Support case during an attack
options.explanation: Shield Standard gives automatic network-layer protection but no Shield Response Team engagement and no cost protection credits.

options.text: Add AWS WAF rate-based rules to the distribution and cap the Auto Scaling group's maximum size to limit the scaling cost
options.explanation: Rate limits and a scaling cap reduce cost but can take the site down under load, and they provide no DDoS experts.

options.text: Enable Amazon GuardDuty in the account and send its findings through Amazon EventBridge to the operations team's pager
options.explanation: GuardDuty detects threats in account activity; it does not mitigate DDoS attacks, engage experts or credit scaling charges.

options.text: Subscribe to AWS Shield Advanced and add protections for the distribution, the load balancer and the hosted zone

explanation: Shield Advanced adds, for the resources it protects, access to the Shield Response Team (which needs a Business or Enterprise Support plan) and cost protection in the form of service credits for usage spikes caused by a DDoS attack. Shield Standard has neither, WAF rate rules with a scaling cap trade availability for cost, and GuardDuty does not mitigate DDoS. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/waf/latest/developerguide/ddos-advanced-summary-capabilities.html

prompt:
Amazon ECS services and AWS Lambda functions share about 300 configuration values, such as endpoint URLs, feature settings and 20 internal service identifiers that must be encrypted with AWS KMS. Values are organized by environment and application, none need rotation, each is under 4 KB, and the company wants the lowest cost.

Which solution meets these requirements?

options.text: Store all 300 values as secrets in AWS Secrets Manager under environment-based names and grant each service read access
options.explanation: Secrets Manager is billed per secret per month and per API call; its rotation features are unused here, so it costs far more.

options.text: Store the values as standard-tier parameters in Parameter Store under /env/app paths, using SecureString for the 20
Store the values as advanced-tier parameters in Parameter Store under /env/app paths, using SecureString for the 20
